strengths: Novel game-theoretic framework: The interpretation of group fairness as cooperative bargaining problem with connection to Kalai-Smorodinsky solution is creative and well-motivated
Strong theoretical contributions: Theorem 3.4 on compactness/convexity of risk sets, complete axiomatic characterizations (Props 4.2, 4.4), and O(1/√n) convergence guarantees are technically solid

Addresses real fairness limitation: Figure 1 clearly demonstrates why absolute-scale methods (minimax regret) fail under heterogeneous group predictability; relative improvement's scale invariance directly solves this
Comprehensive framework: Unifies existing fairness approaches (Group DRO, MMV, MMR) as different bargaining solutions with clear axiomatic comparison (Table 1)
Principled justification: Relative improvement satisfies compelling combination of axioms (Pareto optimality, scale invariance, individual monotonicity) inherited from KS solution
No-harm guarantee: Theorem 4.1 ensures no group worse than baseline, addressing failure mode of minimax regret
weaknesses: Completely absent empirical validation: No experiments on any datasets, synthetic or real; no comparisons with Group DRO/MMV/MMR; no evidence that theoretical advantages translate to practice—critical omission for ICML fairness work

Computational aspects entirely unaddressed: No algorithms provided for solving problem (3); complexity of leximin solution for m>2 not analyzed; optimization in overparameterized regimes acknowledged as open problem (p.8); no reproducible code

Baseline predictor selection not principled: Solution critically depends on f₀ choice with no guidance provided; no sensitivity analysis; different baselines yield different 'fair' solutions; undermines fairness principle
Strong parametric assumptions: Compact Θ (Assumption 3.2) problematic for neural networks; weak compactness requirement (Assumption 3.3) restrictive; generality to broader function classes unclear

Leximin refinement for m>2 feels incomplete: Requires comprehensive closure and modified axioms (SYM', IIIA, IM') without clear intuition; why leximin vs alternatives not explained; complexity not analyzed

Convergence rate limitations: Theorem 5.4 bound scales as C/Δ where Δ = min_g(Rg(f₀)-Rg(f*_g)); if one group has small potential improvement, convergence becomes arbitrarily slow; data-dependent rate weakness undiscussed

Practical implementation gaps: Assumes known group membership without discussing privacy implications; no treatment of intersectionality or subgroup fairness; real-world group definition challenges not addressed
Minimal ethical discussion: Impact statement (p.9) dismissively claims no ethical concerns requiring emphasis; fairness work inherently involves ethical considerations
Limited novelty boundaries: While relative improvement metric and bargaining connection are novel, applying game theory to fairness optimization is not new; mathematical techniques are standard

strengths: Novel connection between fair ML and cooperative bargaining theory, providing elegant game-theoretic interpretation of fairness criteria
Well-motivated problem: Figure 1 compellingly shows when scale-insensitive methods (minimax regret) fail with heterogeneous group predictability
Rigorous theoretical development: Theorems 3.4, 4.1, and Propositions 4.2-4.4 establish solid formal foundations with complete proofs
Unified framework unifying Group DRO, MMV, and MMR as different bargaining solutions, enabling systematic axiomatic comparison (Table 1)
Scale invariance and individual monotonicity axioms provide principled justification beyond ad-hoc fairness constraints
Applicability across regression, classification, and nonparametric settings with concrete instantiations
weaknesses: CRITICAL: No empirical validation whatsoever—zero experiments, synthetic benchmarks, or real-world comparisons. For a fairness paper claiming practical relevance, this is disqualifying and prevents assessing whether the approach actually outperforms simpler alternatives

No computational algorithms or complexity analysis. Authors acknowledge in Section 6: 'we do not address the algorithmic challenges of computing these solutions efficiently.' No pseudocode, runtime comparisons, or guidance for practitioners

Severe limitation to modern settings: Acknowledged inability to handle overparameterized regimes with no proposed solutions. Assumptions 3.2/3.3 require convexity and compact parameter spaces—violated by neural networks, tree ensembles, and modern deep learning
Baseline predictor f₀ selection is critical yet severely underdiscussed—no practical guidance on how to choose it, sensitivity analysis, or discussion of stakeholder preferences

Metric itself not particularly novel: relative improvement is a simple ratio closely related to maximin explained variance (Meinshausen & Bühmann, 2015). Primary novelty is conceptual (game-theoretic interpretation) rather than methodological

Questionable practical relevance of bargaining interpretation: groups don't negotiate in ML fairness; baseline is engineer-determined, not negotiated. The analogy is elegant but loose—more intellectual exercise than genuine game-theoretic model

Multi-group extension (m>2) requires leximin refinement, adding complexity without empirical demonstration that these solutions differ meaningfully from simpler maximin approach or that the refinement provides practical benefits
Convergence rates are standard (O(1/√n)) with potentially problematic dependence on Δ when groups have very small potential improvement—not addressed
Theorem 4.1's no-harm guarantee requires f₀ ∈ F and is relatively weak (essentially: don't do worse than baseline), reducing its force
Presentation gaps: Missing practical guidance on axiom importance, when to prefer RI over alternatives, typical empirical convergence behavior, and computational costs relative to Group DRO

strengths: Novel game-theoretic perspective: Creative and illuminating interpretation of group fairness as cooperative bargaining, providing fresh axiomatic grounding through the Kalai-Smorodinsky solution

Addresses real limitations of existing methods: Compelling Figure 1 example demonstrates how minimax regret fails with heterogeneous group predictability, while RI achieves balanced signal extraction (69%, 69% vs -56%, 87%)
Rigorous theoretical framework: Theorem 3.4 elegantly establishes compact and convex risk set properties; comprehensive treatment of parametric and nonparametric settings with verified assumptions

Strong axiomatic justification: Scale invariance axiom is genuinely important and violated by existing methods; systematic comparison in Table 1 clearly explains why KS axioms (PO, SYM, SI, IM) are desirable for fairness
Natural no-harm guarantee: Theorem 4.1 ensures groups aren't harmed relative to baseline without explicit constraints, addressing a key failure of minimax regret
General framework with broad applicability: Covers regression, classification, and RKHS settings; convergence analysis (Theorem 5.4) with O(1/√n) rates and explicit finite-sample bounds
weaknesses: Complete absence of empirical validation: Only the 2D toy example in Figure 1; no experiments on synthetic or real datasets comparing RI with Group DRO, minimax regret, or constrained approaches. This is a critical gap for a fairness paper intended for practical adoption

Computational aspects severely underexplored: Discussion acknowledges complexity issues for m > 2 but provides no algorithms, complexity analysis, or solver recommendations. Practitioners lack guidance on how to actually optimize the objective, severely limiting usability

Heavy dependence on baseline predictor f₀: Requires f₀ ∈ F for no-harm guarantee, yet guidance on baseline choice is limited to simple defaults. Sensitivity analysis missing; behavior when f₀ ∉ F and impact of poor baseline choices underdiscussed

Problematic dependence on improvement gap Δ: Convergence rate depends on 1/Δ where Δ = min_g[R_g(f₀) − R_g(f*_g)]; small gaps lead to arbitrarily slow convergence. Practical conditions for Theorem 5.4 applicability may not hold without verification

Extension to m > 2 groups is somewhat ad-hoc: Leximin refinement is pragmatic but less elegant than KS; modified axioms (SYM', IIIA, IM') are less standard and intuitive. Alternative extensions not discussed; priority structure for fairness not justified

Overparameterized regime unaddressed: Acknowledged limitation for modern neural networks; strict convexity fails and covering numbers become inapplicable, making Theorem 3.4 conditions potentially violated in practical high-dimensional settings

Limited connection to standard fairness notions: Focuses on risk-based fairness; connection to demographic parity, equalized odds, and error-rate fairness for classification underspecified. Framework may feel unfamiliar to practitioners accustomed to error-rate metrics

Group structure assumptions too rigid: Assumes known, fixed, non-overlapping groups; no discussion of robustness to group specification errors, overlapping groups, or intersectional fairness. Real-world group definitions are often ambiguous

Incomplete empirical guidance: No guidance on sensitivity to baseline choice, scalability analysis, or realistic computational requirements. Figure 3 schematic comparison lacks quantitative detail necessary for practitioners to assess trade-offs

strengths: Novel bargaining-theoretic perspective on group fairness providing unified framework for comparing existing criteria (Group DRO, MMV, MMR); creates conceptual bridge between fair learning and cooperative game theory
Rigorous mathematical development including Theorem 3.4 on risk set convexity/compactness under mild conditions and convergence guarantees (Theorem 5.4) with O(1/√n) rates

Strong axiomatic characterization via scale invariance and individual monotonicity, with clear comparison table showing each criterion's axiom satisfaction; addresses real failure mode of minimax regret
Practical no-harm guarantee (Theorem 4.1) ensuring no group harmed relative to baseline, contrasting favorably with minimax regret
Comprehensive treatment covering regression, classification, and nonparametric RKHS settings with extensive theoretical development and appendices
Compelling empirical motivation showing real problem with minimax regret on ACS income data (North Dakota gap ratio ≈0.10 causing -74% relative improvement for white group)
weaknesses: Core relative improvement metric is not novel—Meinshausen & Bühlmann (2015) already propose maximizing worst-group explained variance in regression; while bargaining connection is new, the fairness criterion itself is a straightforward normalization rather than fundamental innovation

Bargaining framework feels post-hoc: relative improvement could be justified directly via scale invariance without invoking cooperative game theory; bargaining is elegant theoretical lens but doesn't alter practical fairness properties

Critical dependence on baseline predictor f_0 with limited practical guidance for selection; vulnerable to manipulation where groups incentivize worse baselines; Theorem 4.1 requires f_0 ∈ F which may not hold for deployed legacy models

Insufficient experimental validation restricted to linear regression on ACS income data; experiments mainly confirm MMRI achieves equal relative improvement by construction; missing: nonlinear models, neural networks, other domains, and comparison with constraints-based fairness methods (Agarwal et al. 2018)

Computational scalability unaddressed—leximin optimization for m > 2 groups stated to grow in complexity but no algorithms provided, no complexity analysis, no runtime comparisons; significant gap for applications with many demographic groups

Leximin refinement for m > 2 is mathematically sound but poorly motivated; while Roth (1979) impossibility result requires tie-breaking, paper doesn't justify why leximin embodies fairness better than alternative refinements
Overparameterization limitations acknowledged as future work but critical: modern ML (neural networks) violates strict convexity assumptions, substantially limiting applicability
Convergence guarantee (Theorem 5.4) depends on 1/Δ where Δ = min_g(R_g(f_0) - R_g(f*_g)); for low-predictability groups, Δ tiny, making convergence prohibitively slow; no finite-sample analysis

Missing practical guidance: when should practitioners choose relative improvement fairness over equalized odds, demographic parity, etc.? No discussion of fairness notion appropriate for different contexts

Weak impact statement missing discussion of societal consequences, regulatory implications, and when relative improvement fairness is appropriate—particularly important given sensitivity to baseline choice

strengths: Novel bargaining theory perspective on fairness with rigorous connection to Kalai-Smorodinsky solution; compelling motivation showing minimax regret's failure when groups have heterogeneous predictability

Solid theoretical framework: Theorem 3.4 elegantly establishes geometric properties of risk sets under mild conditions; comprehensive axiomatic characterization (Table 1) clearly compares fairness principles
Broad applicability shown across parametric (linear/logistic regression) and nonparametric (RKHS) settings with O(1/√n) convergence guarantees
Strong no-harm guarantee: relative improvement ensures no group performs worse than baseline, unlike minimax regret, with simple principled justification
Extensive empirical validation that problem is real: 73% of 400 ACS configurations exhibit substantial asymmetry in group predictability; clear examples across multiple states and features
weaknesses: Core metric is not novel: relative improvement/explained variance from baseline already proposed by Meinshausen & Bühmann (2015); paper essentially provides post-hoc bargaining-theoretic justification for existing metric rather than introducing fundamentally new principle

Zero algorithmic contribution and no solution methods: paper provides no algorithms for computing MMRI solutions; only experiments use linear models with group reweighting (parametrizing λ ∈ [0,1] which traces frontier but doesn't demonstrate scalable computation); explicitly states algorithmic challenges for m>2 are left unaddressed; practitioners given no guidance on implementation

Framework fundamentally inapplicable to overparameterized modern ML: paper acknowledges uniform convergence guarantees fail when 'standard complexity controls such as covering numbers become inapplicable'; Theorem 3.4 requires strict convexity or convex parameter spaces, violated by neural networks; severe limitation given dominance of overparameterized models in practice

Baseline predictor dependence inadequately analyzed: solution critically depends on f₀ choice but no sensitivity analysis provided; claim in Appendix C that this is a feature (disagreement point in bargaining) doesn't address practical question of how solutions change with baseline; undefined when R_g(f₀)=R_g(f*_g); mapping confounds baseline choice with fairness comparison

Experiments extremely limited in scope: only linear models tested (no nonlinear models, neural networks, or realistic modern ML); only binary 2-group settings (leximin extension for m>2 never validated); only continuous outcome settings; visualizes Pareto frontiers rather than comparing learned models on test sets; no runtime/complexity analysis; unrealistic lambda-sweeping setup

Scale invariance positioned as always beneficial but not universally true: in imbalanced classification, absolute comparisons may be appropriate; relative improvement masks inadequate service to inherently harder-to-predict groups; Nash solution also satisfies SI (Table 1) but paper doesn't explain why KS is preferable; no guidance on when to avoid scale invariance

Incomplete analysis for m>2 case: leximin refinement pragmatically avoids impossibility but less principled than m=2 axioms; new axioms (IIIA, IM') are less intuitive; comprehensive closure requirement adds complexity and unclear when it applies; no empirical validation of leximin extension; no clear comparison of when KS dominates Nash or Egalitarian for m>2

strengths: Novel bargaining theory perspective on group fairness with rigorous mathematical development and elegant connection to Kalai-Smorodinsky solution
Well-motivated problem: comprehensively demonstrates (73% of 400 real configs) that absolute-scale methods fail when groups have different predictability, with compelling North Dakota income example
Strong theoretical contributions: Theorem 3.4's compact risk set characterization, axiomatic framework (Props 4.2, 4.4), no-harm guarantee (Thm 4.1), and O(1/√n) convergence rates
Unified framework elegantly maps existing fairness methods (Group DRO, MMR, MMV) to classical bargaining solutions, enabling principled axiomatic comparison
Thorough technical execution with comprehensive assumptions verification across multiple function classes (linear, logistic, RKHS), detailed proofs, and extensive appendices
Excellent presentation: well-organized, clearly written with effective visualizations (especially Figs 1-3) that effectively communicate main ideas to diverse audiences
Comprehensive empirical analysis documenting gap ratio distribution across 50 states with both single and multi-feature models
weaknesses: Severely limited empirical scope: all experiments on linear regression with single ACS dataset; no classification, neural networks, alternative domains, or nonlinear models despite claiming RKHS applicability

Modest practical improvements in realistic scenarios: Figure 10 shows often-small visual differences between MMRI and MMR outside extreme cases; paper identifies failure mode but doesn't convincingly demonstrate superiority in typical settings
Critical gap: overparameterized regime not addressed despite acknowledged inapplicability of strict convexity and uniform convergence guarantees—significant limitation for modern deep learning

Computational complexity entirely unaddressed: no algorithmic descriptions, complexity analysis, runtime comparisons, or code; unclear whether optimization is tractable for high-dimensional/large-m problems
No empirical sensitivity analysis for baseline choice (f₀) despite acknowledged dependence on this design choice; philosophical discussion insufficient for practitioners
Leximin solution for m > 2 adds complexity; sequential optimization less elegant than m=2 case with no provided complexity analysis
Missing comparisons: no evaluation against other relative fairness metrics, alternative normalization schemes, or engagement with broader fairness literature beyond statistical criteria
